newsitem.title: UK: Big gold miners seek El Dorado around globe.
newsitem.headline: Big gold miners seek El Dorado around globe.

text.p: The world's biggest gold miners, with an eye to expansion, are enthusiastically staking out projects in gold-rich countries recently considered too politically risky for investment.
In sharp contrast, South Africa, still the world's top producer, is struggling to stem a decline in output and the mature industry there holds little interest for expansion.

"There's no question South Africa's market share is going to decline. Exploration going into South Africa is negligible," Tom Dale, managing director of Gengold Ltd, told a gold conference of top mining houses on Thursday.
South Africa used to consistently produce about 600 tons of gold annually, but would do well now to stabilise at around 500 tons per year, Dale added.
Budgets for exploration topped $100 million per year for some of the houses attending the conference, sponsored by RBC Dominion Securities Inc.

"Africa is a veritable treasure house as yet not fully tapped. In the next century, Africa outside of South Africa will emerge as the major gold-producing continent," said Sam Jonah of Ghana-based Ashanti Goldfields Corp.
The political situation in Ghana has improved greatly in recent years and is attracting big mining houses, Jonah noted.
Barrick Gold Corp., which spent the first 10 of its 12-year life as a North American miner, has set out to double in size over the next decade, said chairman Peter Munk.
Munk waxed enthusiastic about South America for its rich gold deposits and recently warmed investment climate. Barrick has interests in Peru, Argentina and Chile.

"In Chile, the raised fist of Che Guevara is a romantic fantasty of teenagers which becomes less attractive when you grow up. This counter revolution has spread and we're going to find a totally different climate there," Munk said.
Barrick completed a C$1 billion ($ ) takeover of the
exploration company Arequipa Resources Ltd last month, solidifying its position as the world's third biggest gold producer and giving it ownership of Arequipa Pierina gold deposit in Peru.
Countries within the former Soviet Union were also slowly sparking cautious interest.

U.S.-based Newmont Mining Corp. chairman Ron Cambre said the company was pleased with its first project in Uzbekistan and was considering a second with similar reserves of around seven million ounces in the Angren mining district.
"We have an aggressive programme in the international arena," Cambre said. "Uzbekistan has excellent leadership. It's a different culture but we're getting better at dealing with it."
Gengold's Dale noted that South African companies were focusing on getting leaner and increasing productivity. "We may look dead, but we're still kicking," he said.

"There's a revolution going on in the South African mining industry," he added, noting it concentrated on paring overhead costs and top-heavy corporate structure, improving productivity and boosting cooperation through mineral rights swaps.
"Successful mining houses will be those who implement change," he said."And if you don't improve capacity utilization, then production will continue on a sharp downward curve."
